---
title: "Interpolating Soil Moisture with Kriging"
date: 2026-09-17
categories: [tool, geostatistics]
description: "Given sparse soil moisture samples, fit a variogram model to how similar nearby points really are, then predict a full continuous surface across the whole field, with its own uncertainty. Runs on R; Python shown as reference only."
---

A soil probe gives you a number at one point. A field has thousands of
points you didn't probe. Kriging is the answer to "what's the value
everywhere else, and how sure am I." It's named after Danie Krige, a
South African mining engineer who developed it in the 1950s to
estimate ore grade between drill holes. Today it's used just as often
for soil moisture, pH, and pollutant concentration: anything measured
at scattered locations, where a full map matters more than the
individual readings.

This is also the first article on this site where Python doesn't run
live. Read on for why, and what it means for how this page is built.

Prefer to skip straight to a result? The
[standalone tool](/tools/kriging-interpolator.html) runs the same
computation: upload your own file, pick the column, and it predicts
the surface for you.

`.shp`/`.dbf`/`.shx` selected together) with a numeric column: soil
moisture, pH, anything measured at scattered locations.

## 2. Why fit a variogram, instead of just averaging nearby points?

The simplest way to fill in the gaps is Inverse Distance Weighting
(IDW): average the nearby points, weighting closer ones more, with the
weight falling off by some fixed power of distance (usually 2). It's
fast and easy to reason about, and this site's [Buffer/Proximity
tool](/tools/buffer-proximity.html) family uses distance the same
simple way. It has a real limitation, though: **the decay rate is
assumed, not measured.** Whether moisture actually changes fast or
slowly with distance in *this* field, at *this* time, is never asked.

Kriging asks it, in three steps this article builds up one at a time:

1. **The empirical variogram**: for every pair of sample points,
   compute the squared difference in their values and the distance
   between them, then average those squared differences within
   distance bins. This directly measures how different two points
   tend to be as a function of how far apart they are. Pairs close
   together should differ less than pairs far apart, if there's any
   spatial structure to find at all.
2. **Fitting a model**: a smooth curve (spherical, exponential, or
   Gaussian; this article uses spherical) is fit to those binned
   points by nonlinear least squares. The fitted curve has three
   numbers worth knowing:
   - **Nugget**: the curve's value at distance zero. Two points right
     on top of each other should be identical, so a nugget above zero
     means measurement noise or small-scale variability the model
     can't (and shouldn't try to) explain away.
   - **Partial sill**: how much *more* the curve rises as distance
     grows. Nugget plus partial sill gives the *total* sill: the
     variance you'd expect between two points so far apart they're
     basically unrelated.
   - **Range**: the distance at which the curve flattens out and
     reaches that total sill. Beyond the range, two points tell you
     nothing about each other; within it, they do, more so the closer
     they are.
3. **Kriging itself**: using that fitted model as the actual weighting
   rule instead of an assumed power law, it predicts a value at every
   point on a grid, as a weighted combination of the sample points
   where the weights come from the model. Solving for those weights
   also produces a **prediction variance** at every grid point: a
   real "how sure am I," which IDW has no equivalent for at all.

## 4. Compute: fit the model in R — runnable here; Python — reference only

::: {.panel-tabset}

## R — runnable in this browser

```{.webgeods-r #kriging-model-r}
#| package: sf, gstat, geojsonsf, jsonlite
library(sf)
library(gstat)
library(geojsonsf)

pts <- NULL
for (candidate in c("/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip")) {
  pts <- tryCatch(st_read(candidate, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(pts)) break
}

if (is.null(pts)) {
  # Deterministic synthetic soil-moisture survey: 45 points scattered
  # across a roughly 800m x 600m field, with a real spatial trend (a
  # band of higher moisture, as if following a shallow drainage line,
  # plus a smaller ripple) and measurement noise on top -- gives the
  # variogram real spatial structure to find, not just white noise a
  # model could never fit meaningfully.
  set.seed(42)
  n <- 45
  lon0 <- 12.4450
  lat0 <- 41.8850
  dlon <- 800 / (111320 * cos(lat0 * pi / 180))
  dlat <- 600 / 110540
  x <- runif(n, 0, dlon)
  y <- runif(n, 0, dlat)
  trend <- 22 + 10 * exp(-((x / dlon - y / dlat)^2) / 0.08) + 3 * sin(4 * pi * x / dlon)
  moisture <- round(trend + rnorm(n, sd = 1.5), 1)
  pts <- st_as_sf(
    data.frame(soil_moisture_pct = moisture, lon = lon0 + x, lat = lat0 + y),
    coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326
  )
  value_col <- "soil_moisture_pct"
} else {
  if (is.na(st_crs(pts))) {
    pts <- st_set_crs(pts, 4326)
  } else if (is.na(st_crs(pts)$epsg) || st_crs(pts)$epsg != 4326) {
    pts <- st_transform(pts, 4326)
  }
  # No column picker in this article (that lives in the standalone
  # tool) -- uses the first numeric, non-geometry column found.
  geom_col <- attr(pts, "sf_column")
  candidate_cols <- setdiff(names(pts), geom_col)
  is_num <- sapply(candidate_cols, function(c) is.numeric(pts[[c]]))
  if (!any(is_num)) {
    stop("No numeric column found in the uploaded file to interpolate.")
  }
  value_col <- candidate_cols[which(is_num)[1]]
}

values_raw <- as.numeric(sf::st_drop_geometry(pts)[[value_col]])
value_mask <- !is.na(values_raw) & is.finite(values_raw)
pts <- pts[value_mask, ]
values_raw <- values_raw[value_mask]

if (nrow(pts) < 5) {
  stop(paste0("Need at least 5 points with a valid value in \"", value_col, "\" -- found ", nrow(pts), "."))
}

# Working/calculation CRS: a variogram fit on raw degrees would treat 1
# degree of longitude and 1 degree of latitude as the same real
# distance everywhere on Earth, which they aren't -- same UTM auto-pick
# (bounding-box center) as this project's other vector tools.
bbox <- st_bbox(pts)
center_lon <- as.numeric((bbox["xmin"] + bbox["xmax"]) / 2)
center_lat <- as.numeric((bbox["ymin"] + bbox["ymax"]) / 2)
utm_zone <- floor((center_lon + 180) / 6) + 1
calc_epsg <- if (center_lat >= 0) 32600 + utm_zone else 32700 + utm_zone
calc_crs_label <- paste0("EPSG:", calc_epsg)

# pts_calc, value_col and v_model (below) stay in this R session's
# global environment after this cell finishes -- the next cell reuses
# them directly instead of re-reading the file and re-fitting, the
# same cross-cell reuse this project's other multi-cell tools already
# rely on (e.g. spatial-classification.qmd's compute cell reusing the
# inspect cell's own `gdf`).
pts_calc <- st_transform(pts, calc_epsg)
pts_calc$.krige_value <- values_raw

# Step 1: the empirical variogram -- average squared difference
# between every pair of points, binned by distance.
v_emp <- variogram(.krige_value ~ 1, pts_calc)

# Step 2: fit a spherical model by nonlinear least squares. The
# starting guesses (range = a third of the max observed distance,
# nugget = a quarter of the data's own variance) are just a reasonable
# place to start the optimizer, not the answer -- fit.variogram()
# refines them against v_emp above.
init_range <- max(v_emp$dist) / 3
init_psill <- var(pts_calc$.krige_value)
v_model <- fit.variogram(
  v_emp,
  vgm(psill = init_psill, model = "Sph", range = init_range, nugget = init_psill / 4)
)

if (isTRUE(attr(v_model, "singular"))) {
  stop("Could not fit a variogram model to this data -- often too few points, or no real spatial structure to find.")
}

# The fitted curve itself, sampled at 100 distances, for the chart
# below.
v_line <- variogramLine(v_model, maxdist = max(v_emp$dist), n = 100)

pts_wgs84 <- st_transform(pts_calc, 4326)
pts_wgs84$value <- pts_wgs84$.krige_value
pts_out <- pts_wgs84[, "value"]

result_out <- list(
  summary = list(
    count = jsonlite::unbox(nrow(pts_calc)),
    calculationCrs = jsonlite::unbox(calc_crs_label),
    valueColumn = jsonlite::unbox(value_col),
    valueMin = jsonlite::unbox(round(min(values_raw), 2)),
    valueMax = jsonlite::unbox(round(max(values_raw), 2)),
    nugget = jsonlite::unbox(round(v_model$psill[1], 4)),
    partialSill = jsonlite::unbox(round(v_model$psill[2], 4)),
    range = jsonlite::unbox(round(v_model$range[2], 1))
  ),
  variogram = list(
    empirical = list(dist = round(v_emp$dist, 2), gamma = round(v_emp$gamma, 5), npairs = v_emp$np),
    fitted = list(dist = round(v_line$dist, 2), gamma = round(v_line$gamma, 5))
  )
)

out <- jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result_out, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
# Attached AFTER the round-trip, not inside it: sf_geojson() already
# returns finished JSON, and a second toJSON() pass would turn every
# scalar inside it back into a one-element array.
out$samplePoints <- jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(pts_out), simplifyVector = FALSE)
out
```

## Python — reference (desktop/server)

**This code doesn't run on this page.** It's real, working `pykrige`,
the desktop/server equivalent of the R cell to the left. See
[why Python can't run here](#why-python-is-reference-only-here).
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from pykrige.ok import OrdinaryKriging

# Reference implementation only -- not executable in this browser
# tool. Constructing OrdinaryKriging() already does BOTH R steps
# above in one call: it computes the empirical variogram internally,
# then fits the model to it.
ok = OrdinaryKriging(
    lon, lat, values,
    variogram_model="spherical",
    verbose=False,
    enable_plotting=False,
)
print(ok.variogram_model_parameters)  # [sill, range, nugget]
```

:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
aCompute = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("kriging-model-r", Generators)
{
  if (aCompute && aCompute.summary) {
    const s = aCompute.summary;
    // Same 5-stop ramp as KRIGE_RAMP above (not a crude 3-stop linear
    // version) so a point's fill is the exact color the surface would
    // show at that spot -- a 3-stop version made most points (anything
    // near the middle of the range) render almost pure white, which
    // read as "not colored at all" against the light basemap. The
    // heavier stroke keeps every point visible as a distinct marker
    // even at that near-white midpoint.
    const valueStep = (s.valueMax - s.valueMin) / 4;
    await sharedMap.setGeoJSON("kriging-r-points", aCompute.samplePoints, {
      type: "circle",
      paint: {
        "circle-radius": 6,
        "circle-color": [
          "interpolate", ["linear"], ["get", "value"],
          s.valueMin, "rgb(166,97,26)",
          s.valueMin + valueStep, "rgb(223,194,125)",
          s.valueMin + valueStep * 2, "rgb(245,245,245)",
          s.valueMin + valueStep * 3, "rgb(128,205,193)",
          s.valueMax, "rgb(1,133,113)"
        ],
        "circle-stroke-color": "#2a2117",
        "circle-stroke-width": 1.5
      }
    });
    await sharedMap.fitToData(aCompute.samplePoints);
    mutable modelResult = aCompute;
    // A freshly fit model invalidates any surface predicted from a
    // PREVIOUS model (re-running this cell with different data, say)
    // -- same reasoning every hand-wired tool's own upload handler
    // uses when new data arrives.
    await sharedMap.removeRasterImage("kriging-r-surface");
    mutable predictResult = null;
  }
}
```

## 5. The variogram, and predicting the surface

The empirical bins below are the direct measurement from step 1 above:
half the average squared difference within each distance bin (that
halving is why the axis says *semivariance*, not just *variance*). The
line is the spherical model fit to them, with its own nugget, sill,
and range marked directly on the chart.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
variogramChart = {
  const m = modelResult;
  const width = 640, height = 220, margin = { top: 20, right: 20, bottom: 36, left: 46 };

  const svg = d3.create("svg")
    .attr("viewBox", [0, 0, width, height])
    .attr("width", "100%")
    .attr("height", height);

  if (!m) {
    svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", width / 2).attr("y", height / 2)
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
      .attr("fill", "#8a8378")
      .text("Run the R cell above to see the variogram.");
    return svg.node();
  }

  const s = m.summary;
  const nugget = s.nugget;
  const sill = s.nugget + s.partialSill;
  const range = s.range;

  const emp = m.variogram.empirical.dist.map((d, i) => ({ dist: d, gamma: m.variogram.empirical.gamma[i], npairs: m.variogram.empirical.npairs[i] }));
  const fit = m.variogram.fitted.dist.map((d, i) => ({ dist: d, gamma: m.variogram.fitted.gamma[i] }));

  const x = d3.scaleLinear()
    .domain([0, d3.max([...emp, ...fit, { dist: range }], (d) => d.dist)])
    .range([margin.left, width - margin.right]);
  const y = d3.scaleLinear()
    .domain([0, d3.max([...emp, ...fit, { gamma: sill }], (d) => d.gamma) * 1.1])
    .range([height - margin.bottom, margin.top]);

  svg.append("g")
    .attr("transform", `translate(0,${height - margin.bottom})`)
    .call(d3.axisBottom(x).ticks(6))
    .append("text")
    .attr("x", width - margin.right).attr("y", 32)
    .attr("fill", "#2a2117").attr("text-anchor", "end")
    .text("Distance (m)");

  svg.append("g")
    .attr("transform", `translate(${margin.left},0)`)
    .call(d3.axisLeft(y).ticks(5))
    .append("text")
    .attr("x", -margin.left).attr("y", margin.top - 6)
    .attr("fill", "#2a2117").attr("text-anchor", "start")
    .text("Semivariance");

  // Reference lines for the three numbers the stat card above also
  // reports -- nugget/sill as flat dashed horizontals, range as a
  // dashed vertical. Drawn BEFORE the curve/points below, so they sit
  // behind the data like a normal gridline; their text labels are
  // drawn LAST instead (after the curve/points), each on a small pale
  // pill (measured via getBBox() once the text exists, then a <rect>
  // inserted just before it) so the number stays legible even where
  // the fitted curve or a point would otherwise cross right through
  // it.
  const refLine = (x1, y1, x2, y2) => {
    svg.append("line")
      .attr("x1", x1).attr("y1", y1).attr("x2", x2).attr("y2", y2)
      .attr("stroke", "#8a8378").attr("stroke-dasharray", "4,3");
  };
  refLine(margin.left, y(nugget), width - margin.right, y(nugget));
  refLine(margin.left, y(sill), width - margin.right, y(sill));
  refLine(x(range), margin.top, x(range), height - margin.bottom);

  svg.append("path")
    .datum(fit)
    .attr("fill", "none")
    .attr("stroke", "#ab502b")
    .attr("stroke-width", 2)
    .attr("d", d3.line().x((d) => x(d.dist)).y((d) => y(d.gamma)));

  svg.append("g")
    .selectAll("circle")
    .data(emp)
    .join("circle")
    .attr("cx", (d) => x(d.dist))
    .attr("cy", (d) => y(d.gamma))
    .attr("r", 5)
    .attr("fill", "#42583c")
    .append("title")
    .text((d) => `distance ${d.dist}m, semivariance ${d.gamma}, ${d.npairs} pairs`);

  const pillLabel = (px, py, anchor, text) => {
    const t = svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", px).attr("y", py)
      .attr("text-anchor", anchor)
      .attr("dominant-baseline", "middle")
      .attr("fill", "#5b5347").attr("font-size", 11).attr("font-weight", 600)
      .text(text);
    const box = t.node().getBBox();
    // White, not the page's own #eee5d2 cream -- that matched the
    // surrounding background almost exactly, so the "pill" was really
    // there but provided zero contrast, leaving the text sitting
    // directly on the gridline/curve with nothing to separate it,
    // exactly the "not well formatted" problem this was meant to fix.
    svg.insert("rect", () => t.node())
      .attr("x", box.x - 4).attr("y", box.y - 2)
      .attr("width", box.width + 8).attr("height", box.height + 4)
      .attr("rx", 3)
      .attr("fill", "#fffdf8").attr("stroke", "#d8cdb8").attr("stroke-width", 1);
  };

  // d3.create() built a DETACHED svg -- getBBox() inside pillLabel()
  // above returns all zeros in that state (found live: every pill
  // rendered 8x4px near the origin instead of wrapping its own text,
  // which is what actually made the labels unreadable), because
  // nothing detached from the document has a real layout yet.
  // Attached off-screen for these three calls only, then detached
  // again immediately after -- OJS's own mount of the node this
  // function returns (${variogramChart} below) is a separate, later
  // append() that will show it in the right place regardless.
  document.body.appendChild(svg.node());
  svg.style("position", "absolute").style("visibility", "hidden").style("left", "-9999px");

  // Nugget at the LEFT edge (it's defined AT distance zero) and sill
  // at the RIGHT edge -- opposite corners, so the two never collide
  // even when close together in value.
  pillLabel(margin.left + 6, y(nugget), "start", `nugget ${nugget}`);
  pillLabel(width - margin.right - 6, y(sill), "end", `sill ${sill}`);

  // Range's label sits just above the x-axis rather than near the
  // top, so it never competes with the sill label above -- anchored
  // away from whichever edge the line itself is closest to, so it
  // never runs off the chart.
  const rangeAnchor = x(range) > width - margin.right - 60 ? "end" : "start";
  const rangeDx = rangeAnchor === "end" ? -6 : 6;
  pillLabel(x(range) + rangeDx, height - margin.bottom - 12, rangeAnchor, `range ${range}m`);

  svg.node().remove();
  svg.style("position", null).style("visibility", null).style("left", null);

  return svg.node();
}
```

${variogramChart}

## R — runnable in this browser

```{.webgeods-r #kriging-predict-r}
#| package: sf, gstat, jsonlite
library(sf)
library(gstat)

if (!exists("v_model") || !exists("pts_calc")) {
  stop("Run the cell in section 4 first -- this step needs its fitted variogram model.")
}

# Step 3: krige onto a regular prediction grid over the points' own
# extent, padded 5% on each side. Cell count is capped by construction
# (25 cells along the longer side) regardless of how large the
# uploaded extent is -- same discipline this project's other
# grid-building tools already use.
bbc <- st_bbox(pts_calc)
pad_x <- as.numeric(bbc["xmax"] - bbc["xmin"]) * 0.05
pad_y <- as.numeric(bbc["ymax"] - bbc["ymin"]) * 0.05
gxmin <- as.numeric(bbc["xmin"]) - pad_x
gxmax <- as.numeric(bbc["xmax"]) + pad_x
gymin <- as.numeric(bbc["ymin"]) - pad_y
gymax <- as.numeric(bbc["ymax"]) + pad_y

grid_resolution <- 25
longer_side <- max(gxmax - gxmin, gymax - gymin, 1e-6)
cell_size <- longer_side / grid_resolution
nx <- max(2, ceiling((gxmax - gxmin) / cell_size))
ny <- max(2, ceiling((gymax - gymin) / cell_size))

xs <- seq(gxmin, gxmax, length.out = nx)
# Decreasing -- north (max) first: setRasterImage's own row-major
# convention puts row 0 at the TOP of the image, i.e. the northernmost
# row, so the grid has to be built in that same order.
ys <- seq(gymax, gymin, length.out = ny)
# expand.grid varies its FIRST argument fastest, matching row-major
# order with x as the column index and y as the row index.
grid_df <- expand.grid(x = xs, y = ys)
grid_sf <- st_as_sf(grid_df, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = st_crs(pts_calc))

k <- krige(.krige_value ~ 1, pts_calc, grid_sf, model = v_model, debug.level = 0)
pred <- as.numeric(k$var1.pred)
var_pred <- as.numeric(k$var1.var)

grid_bbox_calc <- st_sfc(
  st_polygon(list(matrix(
    c(gxmin, gymin, gxmax, gymin, gxmax, gymax, gxmin, gymax, gxmin, gymin),
    ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE
  ))),
  crs = st_crs(pts_calc)
)
bb_wgs84 <- st_bbox(st_transform(grid_bbox_calc, 4326))

con <- rawConnection(raw(0), "wb")
writeBin(pred, con, size = 4, endian = "little")
raw_bytes <- rawConnectionValue(con)
close(con)
pred_b64 <- jsonlite::base64_enc(raw_bytes)

result_out <- list(
  summary = list(
    gridCellCount = jsonlite::unbox(length(pred)),
    meanVariance = jsonlite::unbox(round(mean(var_pred, na.rm = TRUE), 4))
  ),
  raster = list(
    width = jsonlite::unbox(nx),
    height = jsonlite::unbox(ny),
    data = jsonlite::unbox(pred_b64),
    wgs84Bounds = round(c(bb_wgs84["xmin"], bb_wgs84["ymin"], bb_wgs84["xmax"], bb_wgs84["ymax"]), 6),
    min = jsonlite::unbox(round(min(pred, na.rm = TRUE), 3)),
    max = jsonlite::unbox(round(max(pred, na.rm = TRUE), 3))
  )
)

jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result_out, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

## Python — reference (desktop/server)

**Also reference only.** Continues the same `pykrige` object fitted
in the step above: `.execute()` is what actually predicts the grid.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

# Reference implementation only -- not executable in this browser
# tool. `ok` is the OrdinaryKriging object fitted in the step above;
# .execute() is the equivalent of this step's krige() call.
grid_lon = np.linspace(lon.min(), lon.max(), 25)
grid_lat = np.linspace(lat.min(), lat.max(), 25)
z, variance = ok.execute("grid", grid_lon, grid_lat)
```

//| echo: false

bCompute = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("kriging-predict-r", Generators)
{
  if (bCompute && bCompute.raster) {
    const r = bCompute.raster;
    await sharedMap.setRasterImage("kriging-r-surface", {
      bounds: r.wgs84Bounds,
      width: r.width,
      height: r.height,
      values: new Float32Array(base64ToBytes(r.data).buffer),
      min: r.min,
      max: r.max,
      colorRamp: KRIGE_RAMP
    });
    // Points on top of the surface -- see the tool's own moveLayer()
    // comment: setRasterImage() always adds its layer above whatever
    // already exists, which would otherwise hide the actual
    // measurements under the interpolated colors.
    sharedMap.map.moveLayer("kriging-r-points");
    mutable predictResult = bCompute;
  }
}

statCardPart2 = {
  const p = predictResult;
  const box = document.createElement("div");
  box.className = "webgeods-stat-grid";
  if (!p) {
    box.hidden = true;
    return box;
  }
  const row = (label, value) => {
    const dt = document.createElement("div");
    dt.className = "webgeods-stat-label";
    dt.textContent = label;
    const dd = document.createElement("div");
    dd.className = "webgeods-stat-value";
    dd.textContent = value;
    box.append(dt, dd);
  };
  const s = p.summary;
  row("Grid cells", s.gridCellCount.toLocaleString());
  row("Mean prediction variance", s.meanVariance);
  return box;
}

## 6. Why Python is reference-only here {#why-python-is-reference-only-here}

R's geostatistics ecosystem (`gstat`, built on `sp`/`sf`) has been the
standard tool for kriging since long before either language ran in a
browser. Python's closest equivalent, `pykrige`, has no WebAssembly
build anywhere. That's confirmed directly against this project, not
assumed from general knowledge: there is no `pykrige` wheel published
for Pyodide, and none of the usual pure-Python fallbacks
(`scikit-gstat`, hand-rolled `numpy`) reach feature parity with
`gstat`'s fitting routines without becoming a second, untested
implementation of the exact algorithm this article is trying to teach
correctly.

This is a different situation from [Viewshed](/posts/raster-viewshed.html),
this site's other R-only article. There, the Python *library* (GDAL)
exists in principle but isn't in this specific browser runtime's
package index. Here, there is no WebAssembly build of `pykrige` to
load in the first place. That's a harder, more permanent gap than a
narrower one.

The snippet above is real, working `pykrige` code for a desktop or
server Python environment; it just has nowhere to run inside this
page.

## 7. Where to next

- **Just needed the map?** The
  [standalone Kriging Interpolator](/tools/kriging-interpolator.html):
  upload your own file, pick the column, choose a model, done.
- **Want the simpler distance-only version first?** See
  [Buffer/Proximity](/tools/buffer-proximity.html), which uses no
  fitted model, just a fixed distance.

First tool in the GeoStatistics family; more are planned.
